title: Designing classes and interfaces
idea: A well-designed class owns one job, hides its data behind methods that protect its rules, and depends on small interfaces named for the role they play.
points: Start from behaviour: list what the class must do, then the data it needs.
Make fields `private final`, and reject bad input in the constructor.
Use a `record` for small immutable data, such as a parcel's label and weight.
Name an interface for its role, like `RateCard`, and keep it small.

hero.title: Data bag versus designed class

left.title: Data bag
items: Public fields or a setter for every field
Callers compute the cost from its raw data
Accepts a parcel weighing zero kilograms
Returns its internal list for anyone to edit

right.title: Designed class
items: Private final fields, set once in the constructor
Offers cost(), so the rule lives in one place
Parcel rejects bad weight when it is built
Returns a read-only copy of its parcels
Takes a RateCard interface through the constructor

hero.verdict: Expose behaviour, not data, and every rule has one home.

code.title: A shipment, designed
code.caption: An immutable record, a role interface and a class that guards its own list.

walk.text: A `record` with a compact constructor: a parcel without a positive weight cannot exist.
`RateCard` is a one-method role; `FlatRate` is one rule behind it.
Every field is `private final`; the rate rule is injected.
`add` is the only way in; `parcels` hands out a read-only copy.
The class computes its own cost, so callers never repeat the rule.
The zero-weight parcel fails at construction and never reaches the list.

pitfalls: Do not add a getter and setter for every field by habit.
Avoid returning a mutable internal collection; return `List.copyOf` or an unmodifiable view.
Do not prefix interfaces with I; name the role, such as `RateCard`.

quiz.q: What is the first line `ShipmentDemo` prints?
quiz.why: `cost` asks the `FlatRate` for each parcel: 2.0 × 5 plus 3.5 × 5. The sum is a `double`, so it prints with a decimal.

takeaway: Give each class one job, guard its fields, and depend on roles.
